title: Your Team Already Knows What You've Decided About Them
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), August 20, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli relays a conversation with a guest named Dennis about the unconscious 'verdicts' leaders form about team members, snap judgments made on thin evidence that then shape behavior until they become self-fulfilling prophecies. The anchoring example is Dennis's own confession: he decided a new hire wasn't creative after watching him stay quiet in a few brainstorming meetings, then unconsciously worked around him and gathered only confirming evidence until the employee eventually left, leaving Dennis to ask whether he discovered a real weakness or helped manufacture one. The piece's key mechanism is what Dennis calls the 'signal gap,' the idea that leaders transmit both explicit words and an implicit behavioral signal built from mood, tone, and past treatment, and that when the two conflict, people trust the behavioral signal every time, which explains why even correctly worded praise (per Carol Dweck's effort-focused praise research) fails if a leader's underlying treatment contradicts it. Drawing on Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework, Chiarelli and Dennis note these verdicts form as effortless, rarely revisited snap judgments, and close with a four-question fairness test leaders can apply to any judgment they currently hold about a team member.
points: Dennis's core diagnostic concept, the 'signal gap,' identifies why stated praise or feedback often fails: when a leader's words and their underlying behavioral treatment of an employee conflict, employees consistently believe the behavior over the words.

His personal case study demonstrates confirmation bias in real time: after deciding a quiet new hire 'wasn't creative,' he unconsciously excluded him from opportunities and then interpreted the resulting disengagement as proof of the original judgment, a closed loop that ended in the employee's departure.

The piece explicitly avoids relativism about judgment itself, acknowledging that snap assessments are sometimes correct and that fair responses can include additional training or, in genuine mismatch cases, parting ways, rather than treating all verdicts as illegitimate.

Chiarelli extends Carol Dweck's effort-praise research with a caveat: even scientifically 'correct' praise (praising effort, not innate ability) fails to build motivation if a leader's ongoing treatment of the person contradicts the praise's message.

Dennis's four-question audit (recency, evidence basis, whether the person knows the verdict exists, whether they've been told how to change it) gives leaders a concrete, repeatable tool for auditing their own snap judgments about specific team members rather than a general exhortation to 'be less biased.'
quotes: We explore the "verdicts" that people make all the time, especially at work: the judgments that leaders form early, often on thin evidence, and then unconsciously act on until they become self-fulfilling.

Having reached that verdict, Dennis started working around him, leaving him out and leaning on his team, gathering only the evidence that confirmed the original judgment. Jeff eventually left. With hindsight Dennis asked himself: did I discover a weakness, or help create one?
We transmit two things at once: our words, and a second, powerful signal made up of our behaviour, mood and past treatment of a person. When the two conflict, people believe the behaviour every time.
Dennis notes that most of these verdicts are formed as effortless snap judgments and rarely revisited, which makes them both unintentional and durable.

Dennis closed with four tests for whether a verdict about someone is fair: Does it have a recent date? Does it rest on evidence you've actually gathered rather than just your opinion? Does the person know the verdict exists? Have you told them clearly how they could change it?

His practical suggestion is to pick one person, examine the verdict you hold about them, and run it through those four questions. The uncomfortable part is actually acknowledging we might have been wrong about them the whole time.
